title: Ultrasound replaces TSVs: GHz acoustic links through thinned stacks
idea: Substitute copper TSVs with ScAlN bulk-acoustic-wave transducers on each die's backside: data rides 5-10 GHz ultrasonic bursts through ~30 um of thinned silicon to a receiving transducer on the die above, so the stack itself becomes an acoustic waveguide. No TSV etch, liner, fill, reveal or keep-out zones.
why: Fact 6 HBM TSV tax: removes signal-TSV area and TSV-related yield loss; claim ~20-30% lower stack cost if per-link energy stays under ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Infrared light through silicon replaces vertical TSV signal lanes
idea: Substitute signal TSVs with bonded 1310 nm micro-LED / Ge photodiode pairs: silicon is transparent above 1.1 um, so each die shines data straight up through thinned neighbours, with Fresnel zone lenses etched in backside oxide to focus; only a few fat TSVs remain for power.
why: Fact 6: ~90% fewer signal TSVs and their keep-out area; contactless vertical signalling decouples bond yield from data integrity; ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Femtosecond-laser-written waveguides inside glass interposers
idea: Substitute copper interposer RDL with optical waveguides written in 3D inside a fused-silica interposer by femtosecond-laser index modification, evanescently coupled to grating ports on the GPU and HBM base die; waveguides cross in 3D without crosstalk, collapsing many routing layers into one glass volume.
why: Fact 5: interposer hop from ~3-4 pJ/bit toward ~1 pJ/bit, and HBM can sit 20-50 mm away, breaking the shoreline limit on stack count.

title: Sub-terahertz plastic waveguide ribbons replace DDR copper channels
idea: Substitute PCB DDR traces with PTFE/HDPE dielectric ribbon waveguides carrying 140-300 GHz carriers from CMOS transceivers in the memory controller to modules up to 1 m away; each ribbon moves 50-100 Gb/s with no equalization and no connector stubs.
why: Fact 5: DDR5 10-20 pJ/bit to ~2-3 pJ/bit; distance freedom enables rack-scale pooled DRAM, recovering the ~20-30% stranded memory.

title: Flood-lit optical comb clock replaces per-channel forwarded clocks
idea: Substitute every channel's forwarded clock, DLL and PLL with one mode-locked laser that floods the backside of all chiplets at 1.3 um through the silicon; on-die photodiodes recover a common low-jitter clock so data lanes run source-synchronous with no CDR or link training.
why: Fact 7 periphery and Fact 5: removes clock lanes (~10% of pins) and DLL/PLL area and power (~15-20% of PHY power).

title: Air-gap suspended interposer wires: vacuum dielectric instead of oxide
idea: Substitute the oxide/polyimide around long interposer lines with air: a sacrificial polynorbornene layer is thermally decomposed after RDL build, leaving copper lines suspended on periodic posts and cutting line capacitance ~3x.
why: Fact 5/10: wire CV^2 drops ~60%, taking the interconnect share of HBM energy from ~3-4 toward ~1.5-2 pJ/bit.

title: Charge-recycling bus: adjacent lines trade charge instead of dumping it
idea: Substitute rail-to-rail drivers with series-stacked voltage domains across a wide HBM bus: charge dumped by a falling line in one domain recharges a rising line in the next, and resonant LC tanks recycle clock-line energy.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor: interface CV^2 energy down 2-4x at the same swing, shrinking HBM PHY share of accelerator power.

title: Sidewall-written stack wiring replaces TSVs in DRAM cubes
idea: Substitute TSVs with wiring on the stack's faces: dies route pads to their edges, the stacked cube's sides are planarized, then copper traces are laser-direct-written down each sidewall; four faces give ~4,000 lines per cube at 10 um pitch.
why: Fact 6: removes TSV area tax and the TSV process module (~30% of HBM packaging cost), allowing near-standard dies to be stacked.

title: Lid-as-interposer: the heat spreader carries memory signals
idea: Substitute the silicon interposer with the package lid: a copper/AlN ceramic lid with embedded multilayer redistribution bonds face-down onto GPU and HBM tops and carries die-to-die signals, while the organic substrate below handles only power and external I/O.
why: Fact 6/5: deletes a >2,500 mm2 silicon interposer, frees the bottom side for power, and pulls heat out of taller stacks directly.

title: Origami flex interposer folds memory stacks around the processor
idea: Substitute the flat interposer with a 2 um-line polyimide flex bonded at the GPU edges and folded up and over, so HBM stacks mount on vertical walls and above the GPU, tripling the number of stacks within 5 mm of the die edge.
why: Shoreline limit (Facts 5/6): ~3x more stacks per processor without longer wires; memory capacity per accelerator up 2-3x.

title: Twelve volts into the stack, per-die switched-capacitor converters
idea: Substitute hundreds of low-voltage power/ground TSVs with a few TSVs carrying 12 V; each DRAM die steps down locally with a switched-capacitor converter built from the DRAM process's own high-density trench capacitors.
why: Fact 6: power/ground TSVs are often >50% of all TSVs; cutting them ~10x shrinks TSV area, lifts stack yield and cuts IR drop for 16-24-high stacks.

title: Copper nanowire velcro: room-temperature interlocking die bonds
idea: Substitute solder microbumps and thermocompression with electroplated copper nanowire forests grown through porous-alumina templates on both mating pads; pressed together at room temperature they interlock and cold-weld at 5 um pitch.
why: Fact 6 and Fact 3: no thermal budget hit to DRAM retention, a simple press replaces a ~$2M TCB tool, bond yield improves.

title: Liquid-metal-loaded underfill doubles as shield and heat path
idea: Substitute epoxy-silica underfill between stacked dies with an elastomer carrying oxide-skinned gallium-alloy droplets that stay insulating but raise thermal conductivity ~5x; laser-sintering selected regions of the same film turns them into a conductive ground mesh.
why: Thermal and crosstalk limits on 16-high HBM: taller stacks (more GB per footprint) and higher I/O rates with less dedicated shielding wiring.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory racks with YBCO superconducting backplanes
idea: Substitute copper backplane traces with YBCO coated-conductor striplines in a 77 K memory enclosure: DRAM leakage collapses at 77 K so refresh nearly vanishes, and lossless lines carry 100 mV low-swing signals for meters without equalization.
why: Fact 3 refresh (-90%+) and Fact 5 link energy (~5x lower), traded against cryocooler power amortised over a large pooled memory.

title: Photonic base die turns HBM into a fiber-attached appliance
idea: Substitute the HBM base die's electrical PHY with a silicon-photonics base die (microring modulators, Ge detectors, fiber V-grooves), so a stack talks over fiber at ~1 pJ/bit and can sit anywhere on a board or rack.
why: Facts 5/6: frees GPU shoreline and interposer area; memory scales independently of compute and can be pooled for higher utilization.

title: On-package antenna mesh replaces address and command wiring
idea: Substitute command/address wiring to every DRAM die with a ~300 GHz on-chip antenna broadcast network inside the package: the controller transmits each command once, all dies receive it simultaneously, and only data stays wired.
why: Facts 6/7: C/A pins and TSVs (~20-30% of HBM signals) disappear; more ranks per channel without electrical loading.

title: Silicon-core vias: trench-isolated die silicon replaces copper TSV fill
idea: Substitute copper-filled TSVs with pillars of the die's own heavily doped silicon, isolated by an oxide-filled annular deep trench, so there is no copper CTE mismatch and the stress keep-out around each via largely disappears.
why: Fact 6: keep-out zones are a big part of TSV area; removing Cu stress shrinks them several-fold and drops Cu plating/CMP steps; suited to many slow parallel lanes.

title: CVD-diamond interlayers replace silicon spacers in tall stacks
idea: Substitute dummy silicon spacers and mold compound between DRAM dies with 20 um polycrystalline diamond wafers carrying laser-drilled vias, so every bond layer is a lateral heat spreader (k ~1,500 vs ~150 W/mK).
why: Heat limits HBM to 12-16 high: 24-32-high stacks (about 2x GB per stack) at the same junction temperature.

title: Stream seeds, not weights: on-die regeneration of model tensors
idea: Substitute dense weight transfers from HBM with PRNG seeds plus small low-rank/sparse residuals; an LFSR engine on the compute die regenerates the pseudo-random basis and the residual corrects it, so each 64 B of weights crosses the link as ~8-16 B.
why: Fact 5: bytes moved per token and weight capacity both drop ~4-8x for compressible layers.

title: Ship high-order bits, predict the rest on arrival
idea: Substitute full-precision transfers with split-significance links: only sign, exponent and top mantissa bits of BF16/FP8 activations cross by default; a tiny per-tensor predictor fills low bits from local statistics and exact low bits are fetched lazily for sensitive layers.
why: Facts 5/8: ~40-50% fewer bits per value moved; effective HBM bandwidth up 1.6-2x.

title: Memory lives in the top-of-rack switch, not in servers
idea: Substitute per-server DIMMs with DRAM co-packaged inside the rack switch ASIC module and exposed over existing Ethernet/CXL ports as a shared pool with line-rate atomics; servers keep only small local DRAM.
why: Stranded memory (~20-30% idle in clouds): pooling at the switch cuts DRAM bits purchased by ~15-25%.

title: Open chiplet memory socket standard to admit new DRAM makers
idea: Substitute vendor-dominated JEDEC HBM interfaces with a CHIPS-funded, royalty-free chiplet memory protocol on UCIe plus open reference base-die IP, so any new U.S. memory die maker can attach to any accelerator without building a full HBM PHY.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: removes $100M+ of PHY/interface development from a new entrant's path, diversifying supply.

title: Harvest-and-restack business for failed HBM stacks
idea: Substitute scrapping whole 12/16-high stacks that fail final test with a laser lift-off service: stacks are built with a thin absorbing debond layer at each tier, failed dies are released by a laser through the stack edge, and good dies are re-bonded into new stacks.
why: Fact 6 yield loss of 20-30%: recover most of the known-good dies in failed stacks, adding ~10-20% effective HBM supply.

title: Laser-drilled glass interposer with aerosol-jet silver wiring
idea: Substitute the foundry silicon interposer with a 300 um glass sheet: a UV picosecond laser drills through-glass vias and an aerosol-jet printer writes 10 um silver traces and polyimide dielectric layer by layer; a 10-person shop runs it with two tools and a curing oven.
why: Capital intensity: interposer tooling from a >$100M line to <$2M, with enough density for 512-1024-bit LPDDR buses next to a processor.

title: Micro-coax wire bonds bring 50 Gb/s to cheap stacks
idea: Substitute TSVs in wide-IO stacks with standard gold wire bonds that are parylene-coated and then sputtered with a grounded metal shell, turning each into a 50-ohm micro-coax; staircase-stacked LPDDR dies get impedance-controlled vertical lanes from a used wire bonder and a parylene coater.
why: Fact 6: no TSV tax; per-wire rate rises from ~6 to 25-50 Gb/s, letting wire-bonded stacks approach HBM bandwidth at a fraction of the cost.

title: Reclaimed server DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Substitute new DRAM purchases with DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs pulled from decommissioned servers: a small team builds an FPGA or off-the-shelf CXL-controller card holding 8-16 used DIMMs, screens them with an on-card pattern tester, and sells them as CXL Type-3 capacity tiers.
why: Cost per bit and scarcity: reused bits cost ~10-20% of new ones and add supply with zero fab capex during the 4x price spike.

title: Water-droplet self-assembly replaces precision pick-and-place
idea: Substitute the $1-3M precision die bonder with capillary self-alignment: hydrophilic bond sites inside hydrophobic surroundings are patterned on interposer and dies, and a dispensed water droplet pulls each roughly placed die into sub-micron alignment as it evaporates before direct bonding.
why: Capital intensity: alignment tooling ~100x cheaper; coarse, parallel placement raises throughput for a small line.

title: Magnet-aligned nickel-chain film replaces solder microbumps
idea: Substitute microbumps with an anisotropic conductive film whose nickel microspheres are pulled into vertical columns by a permanent magnet during cure, conducting only vertically at 15-20 um pitch; a hot press and a magnet are the whole bonding line.
why: Capital and process: no bumping or reflow line, so a small team can build wide-IO memory-on-logic assemblies cheaply.

title: Contactless memory slot: PCB coil pairs replace DIMM connector pins
idea: Substitute metal edge-finger contacts with arrays of near-field coupled coil pairs etched in ordinary PCB copper on module and motherboard, driven by a small transceiver FPGA/ASIC; modules slide in without contact, are hot-swappable and the slot pitch can shrink.
why: Data movement and capacity: no connector stubs or wear, denser slots per channel, ~2x modules per board area.

title: Printed photonic wire bonds link memory chiplets to fibers
idea: Substitute sub-micron active alignment of optical engines with two-photon-polymerized freeform waveguides printed in place between laser, modulator chiplet and fiber, so one 3D nanoprinter lets a small team assemble optical memory links.
why: Fact 5: optical memory interconnect (~1 pJ/bit) becomes buildable in low volume without a photonics packaging fab.

title: Bookshelf DRAM: dies standing on edge in slotted carriers
idea: Substitute vertical stacking with edge mounting: dies with pads redistributed to one edge stand upright in a laser-machined or 3D-printed ceramic slotted carrier, like books, with each edge soldered to substrate pads at 50 um pitch; ~50 dies per cm of shelf.
why: Near-HBM density per footprint without TSVs or thinning, and each die is independently reworkable so stack-yield coupling (Fact 6) disappears.

title: Poor man's HBM on commercial HDI substrates
idea: Substitute the silicon interposer with a commercial mSAP HDI board (15 um lines) carrying bare LPDDR5X dies flip-chipped within 3 mm of an FPGA/ASIC, running a 1024-bit bus at a modest 2-3 Gb/s per pin.
why: Cost per bit and capital: roughly HBM2-class bandwidth at LPDDR cost without TSVs or scarce CoWoS capacity.

title: Open-source memory base die on 130 nm shuttle runs
idea: Substitute proprietary HBM base dies with an open-source base die (PHY, BIST, repair logic) taped out on low-cost 130/180 nm multi-project-wafer shuttles, so small teams can stack or attach commodity DRAM dies under their own controller.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: base-die NRE from tens of $M to <$200k, enabling new small memory integrators.

title: Projector micromirror chips switch light between memory and hosts
idea: Substitute the electrical CXL switch with a free-space optical crossbar built from a commodity DLP micromirror array that steers fiber-collimated beams between memory sleds and servers; kHz reconfiguration is enough for circuit-switched memory pooling.
why: Utilization: memory reassignable across 32-64 hosts over passive, low-energy optical paths built from cheap consumer parts.

title: 3D-printed micro-spring sockets for test-then-stack dies
idea: Substitute tungsten-rhenium probe needles and permanent bonds with two-photon-printed polymer micro-springs metallized by electroless plating, forming sockets that contact bare-die pads for at-speed known-good-die test and temporary mounting.
why: Fact 6 yield and the tungsten chokepoint: test-before-stack recovers much of the 20-30% stack yield loss and removes W probe dependence.

title: Liquid-metal micro-wells make chiplet memory reworkable
idea: Substitute solder joints with laser-etched micro-wells in the substrate filled with gallium-indium alloy over a nickel barrier; die pillars plunge into the wells for contact, and a failed memory die lifts out cold and is replaced.
why: Yield and cost: rework instead of scrapping multi-die packages, run with dispensing and lamination equipment a small team owns.

title: Electrohydrodynamic-printed copper pillars replace bumping lines
idea: Substitute photolithographic bumping and plating with electrohydrodynamic direct printing of 5-10 um copper micro-pillars voxel by voxel onto die pads, so one desktop printer turns bare purchased dies into fine-pitch flip-chip parts.
why: Capital intensity: replaces a ~$50M bumping line for low-volume memory-on-logic assemblies.

title: Induction-heated bumps bond stacks without baking DRAM
idea: Substitute oven or thermocompression heating with RF induction: bumps carry a ferromagnetic nickel core that heats selectively in a 1-10 MHz field, melting solder at the joint while DRAM silicon stays below ~100 C; the tool is a coil, an RF supply and a press.
why: Retention and capital: avoids thermal stress that widens the leakage tail (Fact 3) and warpage; tool cost ~$50k.

title: Light-powered contactless self-test of bare memory dies
idea: Substitute probe-card test with optical test: each die carries a tiny photovoltaic cell and LED; a light flash powers on-die BIST and the die blinks its pass/fail and repair map to a camera, testing thousands of dies in parallel without contact.
why: Fact 6 yield and W chokepoint: contactless known-good-die test cuts test cost and probe damage, making test-before-stack cheap.

title: Wire-in-resin printed packages stack commodity memory BGAs
idea: Substitute substrate layers and TSVs with a printer-robot that embeds insulated fine copper wire inside 3D-printed resin frames as it prints, routing 3D connections between stacked commodity LPDDR packages and the host board.
why: Capital and density: dense memory modules without new silicon or substrate fabs; prototypes in days by a small team.

title: FPGA retimer that compresses cache lines in flight
idea: Substitute raw transfers on a CXL memory link with an inline FPGA stage doing base-delta-immediate plus zero-run coding of 64 B lines, packing 2-3 compressed lines into each flit in both directions.
why: Fact 5: effective link bandwidth +1.5-2x and expander capacity +1.3-1.8x for typical data, delivered as pure logic design.

title: Flyover twinax cables replace motherboard memory traces
idea: Substitute long PCB memory traces with ultra-low-loss twinax cables terminated right beside the CPU socket, so memory modules sit in a separate sled and each channel supports more DIMMs or longer reach without retimers.
why: Capacity per socket: ~2x DIMMs per channel or memory moved to cooler zones; a small team builds the harness and adapter boards.

title: Rack daemon lends idle server RAM over RDMA
idea: Substitute buying more local DRAM with a kernel swap backend that pages cold memory into idle RAM on neighbouring servers via RDMA verbs, with replicated pages and fast failover.
why: Stranded memory (~20-30%): fleets buy ~15% fewer DIMMs; pure software from a small team.

title: Hydrogen tracer replaces helium for hermetic optics leak tests
idea: Substitute helium mass-spectrometer leak testing of hermetic optical-interconnect and memory packages with 5% hydrogen-in-nitrogen forming gas and low-cost MEMS palladium hydrogen sensors in a sniffer chamber.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): keeps optical memory interconnect packaging running on a non-scarce gas; tester <$20k.

title: XOR-delta page migration between memory tiers
idea: Substitute full-page copies when a hypervisor moves pages between HBM, DDR and CXL tiers with XOR deltas against the stale copy kept in the far tier, sending only cache lines flagged dirty since the last migration.
why: Fact 5: tiering traffic down 60-90% for read-mostly pages, making cheap far memory usable so less HBM is needed.

title: Graded-speed DRAM bins packaged into wide slow modules
idea: Substitute prime-only DRAM sourcing with fab speed-reject and down-bin dies, graded on an open-source FPGA DRAM tester and packaged into wide, slow modules where 2x more chips at lower clock deliver the same bandwidth.
why: Supply and cost per bit: dies otherwise scrapped or discounted become usable supply; +5-10% bits at 30-50% lower cost per bit.
